clinical_knowledge.topic: Suspicious Pigmented Lesion — Malignant Melanoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Suspicious Pigmented Lesion — Malignant Melanoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes performing a STAT diagnostic full-thickness Excisional Biopsy with narrow (1-2 mm) clinical margins down to the subcutaneous fat (CRITICAL RULE: DO NOT perform shave biopsy or superficial punch biopsy on suspected melanoma, as intact vertical Breslow depth is mandatory for accurate oncological staging), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: growing, asymmetrical, multicolored 1.8 cm skin lesion with irregular borders on right calf (Malignant Melanoma)

Key HPI features: 58F presents for evaluation of a changing mole on her right lower leg. States she has had a small brown spot there for years, but over the past 6 months it has doubled in size, turned dark bluish-black with pink patches, developed notched jagged borders, and recently began itching and spontaneously bleeding after drying off with a towel.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 74, BP 124/80. Dermatological exam of right posterior calf reveals a 1.8 x 1.4 cm asymmetric plaque with irregular, notched borders and marked color variegation (shades of jet black, dark brown, grey, and focal erythematous regression zones). Central superficial ulceration present. Dermoscopy confirms atypical pigment network, irregular globules, and blue-white veil. Palpation of right popliteal and right inguinal lymph node basins reveals no palpable lymphadenopathy.
Relevant background/PMH: Mild sun damage, fair phototype (Fitzpatrick Type II), history of multiple blistering childhood sunburns
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Suspicious Pigmented Lesion — Malignant Melanoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Benign dysplastic nevus without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Spontaneous bleeding or ulceration of a pigmented lesion.
management_principles: Perform STAT diagnostic full-thickness Excisional Biopsy with narrow (1-2 mm) clinical margins down to the subcutaneous fat (CRITICAL RULE: DO NOT perform shave biopsy or superficial punch biopsy on suspected melanoma, as intact vertical Breslow depth is mandatory for accurate oncological staging)
Once histopathology confirms invasive melanoma, plan definitive wide local excision according to Breslow depth and discuss sentinel lymph-node biopsy for tumors >=0.8 mm or ulcerated
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 58F presenting with high-risk changing cutaneous lesion demonstrating all ABCDE criteria of melanoma plus spontaneous ulceration/bleeding.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 74, BP 124/80. Dermatological exam of right posterior calf reveals a 1.8 x 1.4 cm asymmetric plaque with irregular, notched borders and marked color variegation (shades of jet black, dark brown, grey, and focal erythematous regression zones). Central superficial ulceration present. Dermoscopy confirms atypical pigment network, irregular globules, and blue-white veil. Palpation of right popliteal and right inguinal lymph node basins reveals no palpable lymphadenopathy.
reference_soap.assessment: Suspicious Pigmented Lesion of Right Calf, highly concerning for Primary Cutaneous Malignant Melanoma.
reference_soap.plan: Perform STAT diagnostic full-thickness Excisional Biopsy with narrow (1-2 mm) clinical margins down to the subcutaneous fat (CRITICAL RULE: DO NOT perform shave biopsy or superficial punch biopsy on suspected melanoma, as intact vertical Breslow depth is mandatory for accurate oncological staging). Once histopathology confirms invasive melanoma, schedule definitive Wide Local Excision (WLE with 1 cm margins for <=1mm Breslow depth; 2 cm margins for >1mm Breslow depth) combined with Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) if Breslow depth is >= 0.8 mm or ulcerated.

learning_objectives: Apply the clinical ABCDE criteria (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation, Diameter >6mm, Evolving/changing) and ugly duckling sign for melanoma recognition
Explain the strict absolute contraindication against shave or partial incisional biopsies on suspected melanoma due to the necessity of determining exact vertical Breslow tumor thickness
Correlate histological Breslow depth with surgical Wide Local Excision (WLE) margin requirements (in situ 0.5 cm, <1mm = 1 cm, >1mm = 2 cm margins)
Identify indications for nuclear/dye-guided Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB staging for lesions >=0.8 mm or ulceration)

teaching.one_liner: A mole that has changed — grown, darkened, developed irregular borders, or started bleeding — meets the ABCDE warning criteria and needs a full-thickness excisional biopsy, not a shave, to measure Breslow depth accurately.
red_flags: Spontaneous bleeding or ulceration of a pigmented lesion

must_ask.say: How has this spot changed over the past six months — size, color, shape?

must_ask.say: Have you had blistering sunburns in the past, especially as a child?
Has anyone in your family had skin cancer?

history.answer: I came in because a mole on the back of my right calf has been getting bigger, turning dark, and recently started bleeding.
I have had a tiny brown spot there for many years, but it really started changing noticeably over the last 6 months.
It is right on the back of my lower right leg, directly over my calf.
It has grown quite quickly over the past 6 months and is now roughly double its original size, around the size of a dime.

history.answer: It is just this one spot on my right leg that is behaving strangely; I have some ordinary freckles elsewhere, but none look like this.

history.answer: It used to be a regular light brown, but now it has turned dark bluish-black with mottled pink spots and ragged, jagged borders.
Yes, over the past few weeks it has bled a few times when I lightly towel off after showering, and it forms a small crust.
It started itching noticeably over the last couple of months, which was what first drew my attention to it.
No, it does not hurt at all, even when I press on it.
It feels slightly raised and firmer than the surrounding skin, but it is not a hard stone or a floppy skin tag.
There is a small pinkish patch right inside the spot, but there is no spreading warmth, swelling, pus, or bad odor.
No, there is no central hole or pore, and nothing like cheesy material ever comes out of it.
No, it never shrinks or swells up depending on how much I walk. It has just steadily expanded.
I wondered if I might have nicked it while shaving my legs, but there was no real cut or previous injury there.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, my weight has been completely stable and my appetite is normal.
I have not noticed any swollen glands or lumps behind my knee, in my groin, or anywhere else.

No, I have never used indoor tanning beds or sunlamps.
I have not tried squeezing it, picking at it, or putting any wart removers or medicated creams on it.
I was hoping it was just an irritated age spot or maybe a stubborn shaving scab.
I am very anxious because my sister had skin cancer removed last year, and I worry this might be cancerous too.
I would like you to do a full skin check and remove this changing spot completely as soon as possible.
